summary:
Tolima is a department of Colombia, and a trans visitor here stands under the national framework. Since the rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025, marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

That framework sits alongside lethal violence. On 14 April 2025 El País reported the case of Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman beaten in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, filmed by onlookers and thrown into a creek, who died of a second cardiac arrest the following afternoon. No one had been arrested in the case at the time of reporting. Her death provoked national outrage and mobilisations against transphobia.

The scale of the killing is national. Hate crimes killed 13 trans people in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, a figure that anchors the risk assessment for Tolima because the sourced material contains no Tolima-specific information.

Some of the targeting is organised and displacement-driven. The Guardian's investigation of 30 July 2024 documents armed groups in Caquetá giving trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed, and circulating "social cleansing" flyers against trans women. The same investigation quotes an activist stating that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide and records those killings as ordinary cases, and reports 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024. Again, the report contains no Tolima-specific information.

The assessment for Tolima therefore rests on the national transfemicide picture and on violence patterns documented in other departments rather than on evidence from this department itself.
tangentialFactors:
The national legal framework and the national violence record move in opposite directions, and a visitor to Tolima should treat them as separate layers. Identification, marriage and adoption rights are settled nationally, while the risk of lethal assault is set by a conflict-adjacent armed-group environment documented in other departments.

Two departments supply the comparative picture. Antioquia, where Sara Millerey was attacked in Bello in April 2025, shows targeted assault in an urban setting with onlookers filming rather than intervening. Caquetá, where armed groups issued death deadlines and "social cleansing" flyers in 2024, shows organised campaigns that push trans women out of towns and, for many, into sex work as the only available income. Neither department is Tolima, and neither report establishes that the same actors operate there.

The recording practice of the prosecutor's office is itself a turbulence factor: an activist cited in the Guardian investigation states that transfemicide is not recognised as such and that such killings are recorded as ordinary cases, which affects how quickly a visitor can expect a killing to be investigated as a hate crime.

Colombia's decades-long internal conflict remains the background condition for the organised violence, and the 2023 and 2024 death totals cited in the sources are national counts, not counts for any single department.
